domain.name: Distributed Systems
domain.description: High-availability replication, event loops, quorum consensus, and horizontal database sharding.

domainCoverage.synopsis: In distributed systems, networks are asynchronous, packet loss is normal, and clocks drift. This volume establishes the mental models from node replication and quorum to fault isolation.

chapters.title: TCP/IP & Linux Socket Networking Internals
chapters.summary: TCP/IP is the foundational transport and internetworking stack that turns unreliable, unordered IP packets into a reliable, flow-controlled, congestion-aware byte stream. Understanding its handshakes, windowing, congestion algorithms (CUBIC/BBR), and kernel socket states explains why real networks stall, drop, or exhaust ports.

chapters.title: Reverse Proxy Patterns & Edge Load Balancing
chapters.summary: A reverse proxy terminates client connections at the network edge, enforces TLS 1.3, rate limits, and auth, and multiplexes requests over persistent upstream pools to backend services using algorithms like Power of Two Choices (P2C) or consistent hashing.

chapters.title: Backpressure & Flow Control
chapters.summary: Backpressure lets a slow consumer signal an upstream producer to slow down or pause, preventing unbounded memory growth and out-of-memory crashes.

chapters.title: Quorum Read/Write Tuning
chapters.summary: Quorum tuning balances strong consistency, tail latency, and fault tolerance in replicated databases by choosing replication factor N, write quorum W, and read quorum R—where W + R > N guarantees read-your-writes overlap.

chapters.title: CAP Theorem & PACELC
chapters.summary: CAP proves a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee linearizability (C) and 100% availability (A) during a network partition (P); PACELC extends this to normal operation, forcing a choice between latency (L) and consistency (C) even when no partition exists.

chapters.title: Read Repair & Anti-Entropy
chapters.summary: Read repair and anti-entropy background repair heal divergent replicas in eventually consistent distributed stores—read repair fixes stale keys on the hot read path, while anti-entropy reconciles entire key ranges offline using Merkle trees.

chapters.title: In-Memory Caching Architecture
chapters.summary: Caching keeps a reusable copy of data so an application can avoid repeating a database query, calculation, or network call. It can make responses faster and reduce database load. The trade-off: the copy may be out of date.

chapters.title: Dead Letter Queues
chapters.summary: A secondary quarantine queue that captures messages a consumer repeatedly fails to process after a bounded number of retries, preventing poison pills from blocking healthy traffic.

chapters.title: Stream Watermarks & Late Data
chapters.summary: Watermarks track event-time progress in unbounded streams, telling stateful operators when a time window is complete enough to emit results—while allowed lateness and side outputs handle straggling events.

chapters.title: Two-Phase Commit
chapters.summary: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) coordinates an atomic all-or-nothing transaction across independent shards or services by splitting execution into a durable `PREPARE` voting round followed by a `COMMIT` or `ABORT` decision.

chapters.title: Rate Limiting Algorithms, Token Buckets & Redis Lua
chapters.summary: Rate limiting enforces caps on request or resource consumption per caller, tenant, or endpoint over time to protect downstream capacity, ensure fair multi-tenant sharing, and blunt abuse.

chapters.title: Graceful Degradation Tiers
chapters.summary: Graceful degradation protects core user journeys during traffic spikes or dependency outages by shedding non-essential features (recommendations, live counts, heavy analytics) in prioritized tiers before core paths fail.

chapters.title: Gossip & Membership Protocols
chapters.summary: Gossip protocols spread cluster state and failure detections peer-to-peer in O(log N) rounds with constant O(1) per-node bandwidth, eliminating centralized membership bottlenecks.

chapters.title: Multi-Region Active-Active
chapters.summary: Multi-region active-active serves live read and write traffic simultaneously from two or more geographically separated cloud regions. Users hit the nearest healthy region via Anycast or latency-based DNS, achieving sub-50ms local reads and near-zero regional outage impact—at the cost of cross-region replication physics, conflict resolution, and 2x+ infrastructure spend.

domainDeepDive.whatIsThisDomain: A distributed system is a collection of autonomous computing nodes that communicate over an unreliable physical network and coordinate their actions by passing messages. Unlike single-node applications operating with shared CPU memory and nanosecond bus latencies, distributed systems must deliver correct, deterministic outcomes across partial node failures, arbitrary packet delays, and unsynchronized physical clocks. The architecture eliminates single points of failure by partitioning and replicating state across fault domains.
domainDeepDive.whyItMatters: Every modern high-scale platform—from payment ledgers and streaming pipelines to distributed databases and globally routed APIs—is fundamentally distributed. Operating at scale means assuming that hardware failure is not an anomaly, but a constant statistical certainty. Mastering this domain transforms an engineer from viewing infrastructure as black-box servers to understanding the exact physical, mathematical, and algorithmic invariants governing data consistency, network partitions, and latency tail percentiles.
domainDeepDive.keyTakeaway: In distributed systems, networks will partition, nodes will crash, and clocks will drift. Never design to prevent failure; design for deterministic fault isolation, bounded blast radiuses, and provable eventual convergence.
coreArchitectureRules: CAP & PACELC Theorem: In the presence of a network partition (P), a system must trade off Consistency (C) for Availability (A). Else (E), when the network is operating normally, the system must trade off Latency (L) for Consistency (C).

The Fallacies of Distributed Computing: Never assume the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the topology is secure, or transport cost is zero. Every remote RPC call is an unreliable network event.

Idempotent State Transitions: In asynchronous networks where packets duplicate and retry indefinitely, every mutating request must carry a unique idempotency key so executing it multiple times produces identical state.

Quorum Intersection Consensus: For strict consistency across N replicas, the read quorum R and write quorum W must satisfy R + W > N. This guarantees at least one node in any read quorum observed the latest write.

Little's Law & Concurrency Limits: Average concurrent requests L equals arrival rate λ multiplied by average latency W (L = λW). As downstream latency spikes, in-flight concurrency explodes, necessitating hard concurrency limits.

failureModes.name: Split-Brain Partition
failureModes.description: A network partition bisects a cluster. Both halves believe the other half is dead, elect independent leaders, and accept conflicting writes simultaneously, causing irreversible data divergence.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce strict quorum majorities (Q = floor(N/2) + 1) for leader elections and writes. Nodes in the minority partition must immediately step down and reject mutations.

failureModes.name: Cascading Retry Storm (Thundering Herd)
failureModes.description: A temporary database slowdown causes client requests to time out. Clients retry immediately, doubling inbound request volume on an already struggling backend and driving latency to infinity.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement exponential backoff with full jitter and circuit breakers. Drop retries at the edge proxy when downstream failure rates exceed 15%.

failureModes.name: Zombie Node Writes (GC Pause Stale Leader)
failureModes.description: A primary node experiences a 45-second Stop-The-World garbage collection pause. The cluster elects a new leader. When the old leader unpauses, it blindly commits stale writes over the new leader.
failureModes.mitigation: Use monotonically increasing fencing tokens (such as generation IDs or Paxos ballot numbers). Storage nodes reject any write with a token lower than the highest token observed.

failureModes.name: Metastable Failure State
failureModes.description: An incident causes internal queues to saturate. Even after the initial root trigger is resolved, the system remains trapped in a degraded state because recovery traffic continuously exceeds throughput capacity.
failureModes.mitigation: Deploy priority load-shedding, cold-start rate limiters, and fast rejection of non-essential queries to allow the control plane to drain queues before restoring full traffic.

whenToUse: Workloads where data volume or compute capacity exceeds the physical limits of the largest single vertical machine.
Mission-critical systems requiring continuous 99.999% availability that must withstand datacenter and availability zone outages.
Geographically distributed user bases where round-trip latency to a single datacenter exceeds acceptable latency budgets (>150ms).
High-throughput ingestion pipelines (millions of events per second) requiring partitioned, horizontally scalable parallel workers.
whenNotToUse: Early-stage products where operational complexity and network latency overhead outweigh horizontal scaling benefits.
Small engineering teams lacking dedicated SRE, telemetry, and distributed tracing infrastructure.
Workloads requiring absolute ACID serializability across complex relational joins where distributed transactions introduce massive latency penalties.
Applications whose entire active working set fits comfortably within a single modern 128-core, 1TB RAM server.

tradeOffs.pro: Strong linearizability prevents reading stale data and eliminates business logic race conditions.
tradeOffs.con: Incurs cross-node network round-trips for every read/write, increasing p99 latency and sacrificing availability during partitions.

tradeOffs.factor: Synchronous RPC vs Asynchronous Message Queuing
tradeOffs.pro: Synchronous RPC (gRPC/HTTP) is intuitive, easy to debug, and provides immediate confirmation.
tradeOffs.con: Couples services in time and availability, allowing a single slow dependency to exhaust caller thread pools and cause cascading collapse.

tradeOffs.pro: Single-leader architectures simplify conflict resolution and guarantee total write ordering.
tradeOffs.con: The leader is a bottleneck for writes and creates failover fail-stop latency spikes during elections.

coreChallenges.title: Network Asynchrony & Packet Loss
coreChallenges.explanation: Ethernet cables, fiber switches, and routers are physical devices prone to congestion, queue bufferbloat, and severed links. Networks delay, drop, duplicate, and reorder packets unpredictably with no guaranteed upper latency bound.

coreChallenges.title: Partial Failures & Undetectable Crashes
coreChallenges.explanation: In a single-process application, a crash terminates everything. In distributed systems, a node can crash or freeze while others continue executing. A sender cannot distinguish between a dead peer, a congested network, or a paused GC process.

coreChallenges.title: Physical Clock Drift & Ordering Ambiguity
coreChallenges.explanation: Quartz crystals on computer motherboards drift by milliseconds every day. Without a trusted global clock, events across nodes cannot be ordered by wall-clock timestamps alone; systems must rely on logical clocks (Lamport, Vector) or atomic synchronized hardware (TrueTime).

coreChallenges.title: The CAP / PACELC Trade-Off Invariant
coreChallenges.explanation: Under network partitions (P), a system must choose between linearizable Consistency (C) and Availability (A). Even under normal non-partitioned operation (E), systems must choose between Latency (L) and Consistency (C).

domainContent.title: Distributed Systems

spark.summary: A distributed system is a collection of independent nodes communicating over an asynchronous, unreliable network to maintain shared invariants across partial failures, packet delays, and unsynchronized clocks.
spark.keyTakeaway: In distributed systems, networks partition, nodes pause, and clocks skew. Design with logical clocks, majority quorums, consistent sharding, and monotonic fencing tokens so correctness holds under failure.

domain.purpose: Learn the physical, algorithmic, and consensus primitives that govern correctness, consistency, and tail latency when state and computation span multiple networked machines.
audience: Software engineers preparing for distributed systems and staff/principal architecture interviews.
Backend and infrastructure engineers building replicated databases, caches, and coordination services.
Technical leads reasoning about CAP/PACELC trade-offs, quorums, and failure recovery.
learningOutcomes: Model asynchronous network physics, latency hierarchies, TCP flow control, and Little's Law concurrency amplification.
Design efficient RPC protocols using Protobuf schema evolution, HTTP/2 multiplexing, deadlines, and idempotency keys.
Order distributed events without trusting wall clocks using Lamport timestamps, vector clocks, and bounded-uncertainty intervals.
Compare single-leader, multi-leader, and Dynamo-style quorum replication alongside Raft leader election and log safety.
Partition state horizontally with consistent hashing, virtual nodes, and hot-key mitigation without cluster-wide reshuffling.
Protect databases with cache-aside, singleflight coalescing, and distributed leases paired with storage-enforced fencing tokens.

learningJourney.title: Foundations & Network Physics
learningJourney.purpose: Ground distributed design in hardware latency hierarchies, TCP transport mechanics, and the impossibility of distinguishing slow from dead.
learningJourney.explanation: Distributed nodes lack shared memory and global clocks. Every remote call traverses NIC buffers, switches, and kernel TCP stacks where packets drop, reorder, or queue behind congestion. Under Little's Law (L = λW), even a brief downstream slowdown multiplies in-flight connections and memory pressure, while partial failures leave a sender unable to tell whether a peer crashed, a packet dropped, or a reply is merely delayed.

ideas.title: Partial failure creates permanent ambiguity
ideas.description: When an RPC times out, the caller cannot know if the server never received the request, crashed mid-execution, or committed the mutation and lost the ACK. Every mutating RPC must be idempotent.

ideas.title: Hardware latency spans six orders of magnitude
ideas.description: L1 cache (~1 ns) and RAM (~100 ns) are dwarfed by NVMe (~10 us), intra-AZ RTT (~500 us), and cross-region RTT (~80 ms). Minimizing network round-trips dominates local micro-optimizations.

ideas.title: TCP guarantees byte-stream order, not message atomicity
ideas.description: TCP sliding windows and congestion control recover lost packets via retransmission, which introduces head-of-line blocking—a single dropped packet stalls all subsequent bytes on that connection.

example.title: Preventing a Little's Law connection-pool collapse during packet loss
example.scenario: A 1% packet loss on an intra-region switch pushed TCP retransmissions and RPC latency from 12ms to 1,800ms, causing inbound API threads to pile up 150x and exhaust OS file descriptors.
example.reasoning: Applied finite per-hop deadlines (150ms), bounded concurrency limits (semaphores/AIMD adaptive concurrency), and exponential backoff with full jitter on idempotent retries, shedding excess load at the edge before thread pools saturated.
example.lesson: Finite timeouts, bounded concurrency, and jittered retries prevent network jitter from cascading into node exhaustion.

reflectionQuestions: When a TCP write succeeds locally, how much of the remote operation is actually guaranteed to have completed?
According to Little's Law (L = λW), what happens to your service's memory and connection pools if downstream p99 jumps 20x?
How do you distinguish a slow GC-paused peer from a crashed peer—or does your protocol avoid needing to?
Where are deadlines propagated across hops so expired client requests stop consuming downstream CPU?

learningJourney.title: RPC & Service Communication Protocols
learningJourney.purpose: Compare RPC and REST trade-offs, binary Protobuf framing, HTTP/2 stream multiplexing, and backward-compatible schema evolution.
learningJourney.explanation: Service-to-service communication trades human readability for compact binary framing, strict contracts, and connection efficiency. Protobuf encodes fields using compact Tag-Length-Value (TLV) varints with explicit field numbers, allowing additive forward/backward compatibility without breaking rolling deploys. gRPC layers Protobuf over HTTP/2, multiplexing concurrent request/response streams over one TLS connection—though a single TCP packet loss still stalls all multiplexed streams.

communicationChoices.useWhen: Low-latency internal East-West microservice calls, strongly typed contracts, or bidirectional streaming.
designFor: L7 load balancing (HTTP/2 pins L4 connections).

communicationChoices.pattern: REST / JSON over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2
communicationChoices.useWhen: Public North-South APIs, browser clients, and cacheable resource-oriented endpoints.

ideas.title: Never reuse or renumber Protobuf field tags
ideas.description: Protobuf identifies fields on the wire by integer tag, not field name. Deleting and reusing a tag causes old binaries to silently misparse new payloads; mark retired tags `reserved`.

ideas.title: HTTP/2 multiplexing needs stream flow-control tuning
ideas.description: Sharing one TCP connection eliminates TLS handshake overhead, but small HTTP/2 window sizes or TCP head-of-line blocking under loss can throttle high-throughput streams.

example.title: Zero-downtime schema evolution across rolling gRPC deployments
example.scenario: A checkout service renamed and changed the wire type of field `3` (`amount` from `int32` to `string`) in a shared `.proto` contract, crashing older inventory pods during a rolling deploy.
example.reasoning: Reverted the in-place mutation, marked field `3` as `reserved`, added `amount_minor_units` as field `7` (`int64`), and deployed consumers before producers using expand-and-contract compatibility checks in CI (`buf breaking`).
example.lesson: Wire compatibility during rolling upgrades requires additive-only field evolution and automated breaking-change checks.

reflectionQuestions: Can older v1 clients and newer v2 servers coexist safely during a 30-minute rolling deployment?
Are gRPC connections routed through an L7 proxy or client-side load balancer rather than a single L4 connection?
How do you prevent a slow streaming consumer from exhausting server-side HTTP/2 send buffers?
Which endpoints carry explicit Idempotency-Key tokens so client retries never duplicate side effects?

learningJourney.title: Clocks, Time & Event Ordering
learningJourney.purpose: Understand why physical wall clocks cannot safely order distributed events and how logical clocks and bounded-uncertainty clocks solve causality.
learningJourney.explanation: Quartz oscillators drift by tens of parts per million, and NTP synchronization can jump backward (`step`) or slew unpredictably across asymmetric network paths. Using wall-clock Last-Write-Wins (LWW) timestamps silently drops concurrent writes when one node's clock lags by even 50ms. Lamport timestamps establish a partial causal order (`a -> b => L(a) < L(b)`), Vector Clocks detect true concurrency (`a || b`), and Google's TrueTime bounds physical clock uncertainty `[earliest, latest]` via GPS and atomic clocks.

benefits: Sufficient for approximate log correlation and TTL expiration.
costs: NTP backward jumps and clock skew silently discard newer writes in LWW.

benefits: Captures exact happens-before causality without synchronized hardware.
Vector clocks explicitly flag conflicting concurrent updates for merge/CRDT resolution.
costs: Lamport timestamps cannot tell if two events were concurrent.
Vector clocks grow O(N) with the number of writing actors/replicas.

benefits: Combines physical time proximity with monotonic logical counters (HLC).
Enables external consistency (commit-wait) when uncertainty ε is bounded.
costs: TrueTime requires specialized GPS/atomic clock hardware.
Commit-wait adds 2ε latency to write transactions.

example.title: Silent data loss from NTP skew in a Last-Write-Wins profile store
example.scenario: A user updated their shipping address on Node A (clock ahead by 120ms) and immediately corrected a typo on Node B (clock behind by 80ms). The correction vanished.
example.reasoning: Because the store used physical wall-clock LWW (`updated_at`), Node B's newer write carried a smaller timestamp and was silently overwritten by Node A's stale replica. Replacing wall-clock LWW with Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) and per-key version vectors preserved causal ordering and surfaced concurrent edits.
example.lesson: Never use unsynchronized wall-clock timestamps for conflict resolution or distributed ordering; use logical clocks or causal version vectors.

reflectionQuestions: If an NTP daemon steps a server's clock backward by 200ms, what invariants in your codebase break?
Are you measuring elapsed durations with a monotonic clock (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) rather than wall time (`CLOCK_REALTIME`)?
When two replicas accept concurrent offline writes, does your system silently drop one (LWW) or preserve both via vector clocks/CRDTs?
How does your database assign snapshot read timestamps without stale reads across regions?

learningJourney.title: Replication & Consensus Models
learningJourney.purpose: Compare single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless quorum replication, and master how Raft guarantees safety across partitions.
learningJourney.explanation: Replication improves durability and read scale, but introduces divergence risk. Single-leader replication orders writes at one primary and ships WAL/binlog entries to followers (sync or async). Multi-leader accepts writes in multiple regions but requires conflict resolution. Leaderless Dynamo-style clusters write to W and read from R of N replicas, achieving overlap when `R + W > N`. For linearizable state (metadata, locks, ledgers), Raft consensus uses randomized election timeouts, term numbers, and strict majority quorums (`floor(N/2) + 1`) so at most one leader is elected per term and committed entries are never lost.

ideas.title: Quorum R + W > N alone does not guarantee linearizability
ideas.description: Under concurrent writes or sloppy quorums/hinted handoff, Dynamo-style quorums can return stale values unless paired with read-repair, anti-entropy Merkle trees, and causal versioning.

ideas.title: Raft safety hinges on the Leader Completeness property
ideas.description: A candidate can only win an election if its log is at least as up-to-date as a majority of voters, guaranteeing the new leader already holds every previously committed entry.

ideas.title: Async replication risks committed data loss on failover
ideas.description: Promoting a lagging async follower after a primary crash drops acknowledged writes; semi-synchronous replication (waiting for at least one follower ACK) bounds loss at the cost of write latency.

example.title: Preventing split-brain during an asymmetric datacenter partition in Raft
example.scenario: A 5-node etcd cluster split into a 2-node minority (including the old leader) and a 3-node majority after a top-of-rack switch failure.
example.reasoning: The 3-node majority incremented the Raft term, elected a new leader, and continued committing writes. Meanwhile, the old leader in the 2-node minority could not gather 3 ACKs for heartbeats or AppendEntries, stepped down via CheckQuorum, and rejected stale reads/writes—preventing split-brain divergence.
example.lesson: Odd-numbered majority quorums (`floor(N/2) + 1`) ensure at most one partition can ever elect a leader or commit state.

caveats: Read-only queries served by a Raft leader still risk stale reads if the leader was partitioned and has not confirmed its lease/ReadIndex with a quorum.
Multi-leader replication shifts complexity from failover availability to deterministic conflict resolution.
reflectionQuestions: Under CAP/PACELC, does this workload choose Consistency or Availability during a partition, and Latency or Consistency in normal operation?
If the primary database crashes right after acknowledging a write, can an async replica lose that transaction on promotion?
How does a Raft leader serve linearizable reads without writing a no-op entry to the log on every read?
Why is a 4-node consensus cluster no more fault-tolerant than a 3-node cluster?

learningJourney.title: Distributed Data Partitioning & Sharding
learningJourney.purpose: Scale storage and throughput horizontally using consistent hash rings, virtual nodes, range partitioning, and hot-key mitigation.
learningJourney.explanation: Naive `hash(key) % N` sharding fails catastrophically when `N` changes, relocating nearly 100% of keys and triggering database stampedes. Consistent hashing maps both nodes and keys onto a `0..2^32-1` ring so adding or removing a node moves only `K/N` keys between immediate neighbors. Virtual nodes (vnodes) assign many ring tokens per physical machine to smooth key variance and weight heterogeneous hardware, while range partitioning supports efficient range scans at the risk of sequential hot-spots.

benefits: Uniform key distribution across heterogeneous nodes.
Adding or removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys.
costs: Cannot execute ordered range queries without scatter-gather across all shards.
Celebrity/hot keys still overload a single shard.

benefits: Supports fast contiguous range scans (`WHERE timestamp BETWEEN ...`).
Easy to split hot ranges dynamically (like Spanner/CockroachDB).
costs: Monotonic keys (timestamps, auto-increment IDs) concentrate all writes on the newest tail shard.

ideas.title: Mitigate hot keys with salting or bounded-load hashing
ideas.description: Consistent hashing balances average key count, not request QPS. For viral celebrity keys, append a small bounded suffix (`key#0..k`) for reads/writes or use consistent hashing with bounded loads.

ideas.title: Decouple logical shards from physical nodes
ideas.description: Pre-allocating fixed logical partitions (e.g., 4,096 hash slots in Redis Cluster) lets you rebalance whole slots between physical hosts without rehashing individual keys.

example.title: Eliminating shard skew and migration stampedes in a 64-node cache cluster
example.scenario: A 64-node Memcached fleet using `hash(key) % 64` suffered a 98% cache miss storm and PostgreSQL overload whenever a single node rebooted, and uneven hardware sizes left some nodes at 90% RAM while others sat at 40%.
example.reasoning: Migrated to a consistent hash ring with 256 virtual nodes per 64GB host (and 512 vnodes for 128GB hosts). Node loss now relocated only ~1.5% of keys to adjacent vnodes, and key-salting (`hot_key#0..7`) spread viral product lookups across 8 shards.
example.lesson: Consistent hashing bounds key movement to K/N, while virtual nodes and key-salting cure physical skew and hot-key traffic spikes.

reflectionQuestions: What percentage of keys must move if you scale your cluster from 10 nodes to 11 nodes?
How many virtual nodes per physical host are needed to keep standard deviation of key load under 5%?
If one tenant or celebrity key receives 30% of all QPS, how do you prevent that single shard from saturating?
Do your access patterns require range scans (favoring range partitioning) or point lookups (favoring hash partitioning)?

learningJourney.title: Caching & In-Memory Architectures
learningJourney.purpose: Design read/write caching topologies that protect origin databases from thundering herds, penetration, and stale-write races.
learningJourney.explanation: In-memory caches cut read latency from milliseconds to sub-millisecond, but introduce coherence and stampede hazards. Cache-aside lets the application manage misses and keeps the cache off the critical write path, whereas read-through/write-through delegate origin I/O to the cache provider. Write-back buffers writes in RAM for extreme throughput at the risk of data loss on node crash. Under high concurrency, expiring a hot key triggers a cache stampede unless guarded by singleflight request coalescing or probabilistic early expiration.

ideas.title: Stop cache stampedes with Singleflight + probabilistic refresh
ideas.description: Singleflight coalesces 5,000 concurrent cache misses for the same key into 1 origin database query, while jittered TTLs and XFetch probabilistic early refresh renew hot keys before they expire.

ideas.title: Guard against cache penetration on non-existent keys
ideas.description: Repeated queries for missing IDs bypass the cache and hammer the database. Cache explicit null tombstones with short TTLs or place an in-memory Bloom filter in front of the origin.

ideas.title: Avoid write-invalidation races
ideas.description: Concurrent read-miss + write updates can leave stale data in cache if a slow miss overwrites a newer invalidation. Use versioned/fenced `SET` or CDC-driven invalidation.

example.title: Defeating a midnight TTL thundering herd on a flash-sale catalog
example.scenario: Every night at 00:00 UTC, 20,000 cached product pages expired simultaneously, sending 80,000 concurrent SQL queries to PostgreSQL and crashing the primary.
example.reasoning: Added ±15% random TTL jitter to spread expirations, wrapped cache-miss origin fetches in Go `singleflight.Group` so only 1 goroutine queried Postgres per key, and enabled stale-while-revalidate serving for 30 seconds during background refresh.
example.lesson: TTL jitter, singleflight coalescing, and stale-while-revalidate turn catastrophic cache expirations into flat origin load.

caveats: Write-back (write-behind) caching risks permanent data loss if a cache node crashes before flushing dirty pages to durable storage.
L1 in-process caches eliminate network hops but require pub/sub invalidation or ultra-short TTLs to bound cross-pod staleness.
reflectionQuestions: If 10,000 concurrent requests miss on the exact same expired key, how many queries hit your database?
How do you prevent queries for non-existent IDs (penetration) from bypassing the cache?
Can a slow read-miss populate the cache with stale data after a concurrent write already invalidated it?
What happens to database CPU if the entire Redis cluster restarts cold?

learningJourney.title: Distributed Locking & Coordination
learningJourney.purpose: Coordinate exclusive access across machines using consensus-backed leases and monotonically increasing fencing tokens.
learningJourney.explanation: Single-node mutexes fail across machines, and naive Redis `SET NX EX` locks fail when a lock holder experiences a Stop-The-World GC pause or VM stall: its TTL expires, Node B acquires the lock, and Node A resumes and corrupts shared state. Safe distributed locking requires two layers: (1) a consensus-backed lease service (etcd/ZooKeeper) with active keep-alive heartbeats, and (2) a monotonically increasing fencing token (e.g., etcd `mod_revision`) passed to the storage engine, which rejects any write carrying a token lower than the highest seen.

architectureFlow.name: Consensus Lock Service (etcd / ZooKeeper)
architectureFlow.description: Grants a time-bounded lease via Raft/Zab and returns a monotonically increasing fencing token (e.g., token = 33).

architectureFlow.name: Lock Holder (Worker A)
architectureFlow.description: Renews the lease via heartbeat while executing work; attaches token = 33 to every downstream storage mutation.

architectureFlow.name: Lease Expiry & New Holder (Worker B)
architectureFlow.description: If Worker A freezes in a GC pause, the lease expires and Worker B acquires the lock with higher token = 34.

architectureFlow.name: Fenced Storage Engine
architectureFlow.description: Processes Worker B's write (token = 34) and rejects Worker A's late zombie write (token = 33 < 34).

ideas.title: Fencing tokens are mandatory for correctness, not optional
ideas.description: Without storage-side fencing token validation, no distributed lock—not even Redlock or etcd—can prevent a GC-paused zombie client from overwriting a newer lock holder's state.

ideas.title: Distinguish efficiency locks from correctness locks
ideas.description: If a duplicate execution merely wastes a few cents of compute (efficiency), a simple Redis lease suffices. If duplicate execution corrupts money or inventory (correctness), you need Raft leases + fencing tokens.

example.title: Stopping zombie-worker overwrites during JVM GC pauses
example.scenario: A distributed cron scheduler used a 10-second Redis `SET NX PX` lock to ensure only one worker compacted a billing file. During a 14-second JVM GC pause on Worker A, Worker B acquired the lock; Worker A then woke up and overwrote Worker B's output.
example.reasoning: Migrated lock coordination to etcd leases that returned a monotonic `revision` as a fencing token, and added an optimistic compare-and-swap check (`WHERE fencing_token < :new_token`) on the metadata store. When Worker A woke up with token 41 after Worker B wrote with token 42, the database rejected Worker A's stale write.
example.lesson: A distributed lock without a storage-enforced fencing token cannot guarantee mutual exclusion across process pauses.

caveats: Redlock relies on bounded clock drift across independent Redis primaries and provides no fencing token, making it unsafe for strict correctness locks.
Keep lease TTLs and renewal intervals tuned so transient 1-second network blips do not cause unnecessary lock churn.
reflectionQuestions: If the current lock holder freezes for 2x the lease TTL due to a GC pause or VM live-migration, what stops it from writing when it resumes?
Does your downstream database or object store actually validate and reject stale fencing tokens?
Is this lock protecting strict correctness (requiring consensus + fencing) or merely avoiding duplicate work (efficiency)?
What happens if the lock service itself becomes partitioned from half the workers?

endToEndExample.title: Put Distributed Systems together: Globally Partitioned Wallet & Ledger
endToEndExample.scenario: A fintech wallet platform serves 50M users across US and EU regions, requiring <50ms local balance reads, zero double-spend under network partitions, and resilience against cache stampedes and zombie workers.

architectureFlow.name: gRPC Edge & Idempotency Gateway
architectureFlow.responsibility: Multiplexes Protobuf/HTTP2 calls, propagates strict deadlines, and deduplicates retries via Idempotency-Key.

architectureFlow.name: Consistent-Hashed Redis Tier
architectureFlow.responsibility: Serves hot balance reads across 256-vnode shards using singleflight coalescing and jittered TTLs.

architectureFlow.name: Raft-Replicated Ledger Shards
architectureFlow.responsibility: Partitions accounts by home region; commits debits/credits through 3- or 5-node Raft majority quorums.

architectureFlow.name: Etcd Lease & Fenced Settlement Worker
architectureFlow.responsibility: Coordinates end-of-day batch settlement with Raft leases and monotonic fencing tokens validated by storage.

reasoning: Account shards are partitioned by user ID on a consistent hash ring with vnodes, keeping cross-shard operations rare.
Within each shard, Raft majority quorums (`floor(N/2) + 1`) prevent split-brain double-spends during AZ partitions (CP under CAP).
Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) order ledger audit events causally without trusting NTP wall-clock synchronization.
Singleflight coalescing and TTL jitter shield Raft leaders from midnight cache-expiry stampedes.
Settlement workers attach etcd fencing tokens to every batch commit so a GC-paused worker can never overwrite a newer settlement.
lessons: Combine CP consensus where invariants are strict (money) with AP/cached reads where bounded staleness is acceptable.
Every layer—network deadlines, idempotency keys, quorums, vnodes, and fencing tokens—addresses a distinct physical failure mode.
Correctness under failure comes from mathematical invariants (`R + W > N`, monotonic tokens), not hoping networks stay healthy.

failureScenario.title: Cross-AZ Partition + Zombie Settlement Worker
failureScenario.reasoning: An availability zone loses network connectivity while a settlement worker inside it is mid-GC pause. Naive single-node locks or async replication would allow split-brain commits or stale zombie overwrites.
failureScenario.recovery: The minority AZ's Raft followers cannot form a majority quorum and reject writes; the healthy majority elects a new leader, issues a higher fencing token to a healthy worker, and the storage engine rejects the old worker's stale token when it unpauses.

decisionFramework.question: Under CAP/PACELC, what does this operation trade off during a partition and during normal operation?
decisionFramework.reason: Choose CP (linearizable quorum) for financial/inventory invariants and AP (eventual convergence) for feeds, analytics, or counters.

decisionFramework.question: Are all mutating RPCs idempotent and bounded by propagated deadlines?
decisionFramework.reason: Network timeouts leave completion ambiguous; idempotency keys make retries safe, and deadlines stop Little's Law queue explosions.

decisionFramework.question: Does ordering depend on physical wall clocks or causal logical clocks?
decisionFramework.reason: NTP skew and backward steps corrupt wall-clock LWW; use Lamport, Vector, or Hybrid Logical Clocks for causal correctness.

decisionFramework.question: How does data partitioning handle node churn and hot keys?
decisionFramework.reason: Use consistent hashing with virtual nodes to bound reshuffling to K/N, and salt or bound-load celebrity keys.

decisionFramework.question: If a lock holder or leader stalls in a GC pause, what enforces mutual exclusion?
decisionFramework.reason: Pair consensus leases with monotonically increasing fencing tokens validated at the storage layer.

knowledgeCheck.question: A distributed cron job uses Redis `SET lock_key worker_id NX EX 30` to guarantee only one worker processes a billing batch. During a 40-second JVM GC pause on Worker A, Worker B acquires the lock and begins writing. When Worker A resumes, how do you prevent it from corrupting Worker B's writes?

options.text: Increase the Redis lock TTL from 30 seconds to 5 minutes so GC pauses never exceed it.
options.feedback: Increasing TTL merely reduces probability while delaying crash recovery by 5 minutes; arbitrary network delays or long pauses can still exceed any fixed TTL.

options.text: Issue a monotonically increasing fencing token from a consensus lock service (like etcd) and have the storage layer reject writes with a token lower than the highest seen.
options.feedback: Correct. Storage-enforced monotonic fencing tokens guarantee that even if a paused client wakes up after its lease expired, its stale writes are rejected.

options.text: Synchronize all worker clocks with NTP every second so both workers agree on exact expiration time.
options.feedback: Clock synchronization does not stop a paused process from executing stale instructions after it already checked the clock before pausing.
